Inherited from Old Norse ek (“I”), from Proto-Germanic *ek (“I”), from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂óm (“I”). The form represents dialectal developments in which the final consonant disappeared and the vowel developed into /æː/. The related form æg (“I”) retains the final consonant.

1001821.etyen:
Related to florentiner (“Florentine; person from Florence”), ultimately from Latin Flōrentīnus (“Florentine; of or belonging to Florence”), from Flōrentia (“Florence”) with the relational suffix -īnus. The coin name is a substantivized form meaning “Florentine [coin]”. The precise route by which the word entered Norwegian is uncertain.
Compare French florentin, historically also used for a coin originating in Florence, as well as the related Norwegian coin name florin.

1004381.etyen:
From the officially standardized Norwegian place-name element Trifan-, representing a local adaptation of Russian Трифон (Trifon), from Ancient Greek Τρύφων (Trúphōn, “delicate; one who lives softly or luxuriously”), ultimately from Ancient Greek τρυφάω (trupháō, “to live softly or luxuriously”), itself from Ancient Greek τρυφή (truphḗ, “softness, delicacy; luxury”), and the definite feminine singular of hule (“cave”). The name refers to Saint Tryphon of Pechenga.
Compare Kven Triffananlaassa and Northern Sami Triffanlåsis, the Kven and Northern Sami names of the same cave.
